The house resumed from April 12 consideration in committee of Bill No. 198, to amend the Customs Act-Mr. Euler-Mr. Johnston in the chair.
On section 1-Vessels found hovering in territorial waters may be boarded and brought into port.
Is the minister going to leave the words "bring to" as they are?

speakeroldname: Hon. W. D. EULER (Minister of National Revenue):
speechtext: We had some debate yesterdaj' as to the propriety of those words, which are intended to indicate that a vessel should come to a stop. Yesterday I was rather in agreement with the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough (Mr. Duff) with regard to the words "heave to" rather than the words "bring to", but I think we might settle the dispute if we adopt some different words which will be perfectly clear. For that reason I move, seconded by Mr. Lapointe, that the words "bring to" in line thirteen be struck out and that the words "proceed to come to a stop" be substituted therefor. I think that should meet all objections.

Before the amendment carries, I am afraid the minister does not realize what those words mean. You cannot bring a ship
at sea to a stop without great danger to the passengers, the crew and the cargo, whether it is a sailing ship or a steamer. In the case of a sailing ship the words "heave to" are correct; they mean that the vessel comes into the wind and proceeds gradually. In the case of a steamer the words "slow down" are proper, because if a steamer stopped and got into the trough of the sea, or if the wind were ahead and she went backwards, she might capsize and founder. Consequently I think the amendment is not in accordance with marine rules and usage.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I would have hesitated to venture an opinion with reference to language of this kind if I had not had the benefit of the views of an officer of my department with regard to the expression "bring to". I am told that the expression "bring to" is defined by Todd and Whall on Seamanship as an order from one ship to another to heave to. that it may be boarded or spoken. Evidently the distinction is that "bring to" is a special expression while "heave to" is a general expression. The Admiralty Manual of Seamanship defines "bring to" as an expression used in bending sails or when a ship is about to anchor, and I am also told that this expression has been used in Dominion legislation for some time past. Still, I have no objection to seconding the amendment of my hon. friend.

I took some trouble this morning to get advice with regard to this expression from those who should know. After all it is a small matter, and I do not think there should be any doubt as to what is intended. In answer to my hon. friend from Antigonish-Guysborough I would say that the words "proceed to come to a stop" does not indicate any sudden effort to stop; I think it will answer the requirements of sailing vessels as well as steamers.

"Come to a stop" means that eventually the ship will stop, but it is a dangerous thing for any preventive ship belonging to any government to order either a sailing vessel or a steamer to stop in the middle of the ocean. That is a dangerous proceeding, and it is not fair to the owners of ships, because it will endanger the lives of the crews and subject the ships themselves to great hazard.
Amendment agreed to.

I understand that the

Customs Act Amendment

I was not trying to bind

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I am sorry I was not
here last night, but I read Hansard this morning and I think my hon. friend has made a slight mistake. It was he who suggested that I should express some view in the matter.
No, it was the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
It does not matter very
much anyway. I was not here on Tuesday either, but I took the opportunity this morning to read Hansard in order to see what took place on the other two occasions. The view's of my hon. friend are about the same as those set forth in this house in 1923, when as Minister of Marine and Fisheries I introduced some legislation with regard to the north Pacific halibut fisheries. That legislation was designed to put into force the provisions of the treaty with the United States concerning the protection of the halibut fisheries in north Pacific waters. Both in the treaty and in the statute adopted by this house there was a provision which conferred extraterritorial jurisdiction upon the enactment of parliament. I mention the fact that this was in the treaty also because that treaty was ratified by His Majesty the King, and no one either in England or in Canada challenged the right of Canada in that respect, and that statute never has been challenged since. It has been enforced since, giving the right to our officers to seize vessels, even on the high seas, which are engaged in fishing halibut in the prohibited zone during the prohibited season. However, at that time the same objection was raised against that statute, and I am free to admit that my hon. friend can quote authority in support of his con-tent'on. It is a debatable question in some respects; it has been debated, but I believe that the trend of constitutional authority is now rather to the effect that t.he dominions have the same right within their sphere of legislation as the Imperial parliament has within its sphere. This view is specially supported in the case of the award re Cooks' and Stewards' Union. That was a New' Zealand case, in which the court decided that the award of a New Zealand court of arbitration as to wages to be paid on vessels trading between New Zealand and Australia was binding with reference to vessels registered in New' Zealand.
In the well known Canadian case of Cain versus Gilhula, where aliens had been deported under the Canadian legislation with regard to alien labour, for having come to this country

in contravention of our law, those men took proceedings by wray of habeas corpus, and the court of first instance decided that as there was a question of extraterritoriality involved our statute was not constitutional; but the Privy Council decided otherwise, and that Canada may exert extraterritorial powers for the purpose of exercising her sovereign powers as effectively as the Imperial authority.
There have been two cases decided by the Supreme Court of Canada, in re Frederick Gerring and re North, in which vessels had been captured outside the three-mile limit, taken in hot pursuit, and the seizure was declared valid by the supreme court.
Different circumstances.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I admit that the circumstances may be a little different, but still the extraterritoriality was admitted in that case. My hon. friend is right as to the point that there is a certain element of doubt attached to the matter, and it is for that reason that in 1920, I believe, the then government submitted to parliament the resolution for the purpose of amending the British North America Act, in order that it should be made clear that any enactment of this parliament within its jurisdiction had the same effect with regard to extraterritorial rights as an enactment of the Imperial parliament. The resolution was adopted by the parliament of Canada in 1920, but I see in the correspondence that there was some difficulty as to the drafting of the resolution or 'rather of the legislation to be introduced in the Imperial parliament. There was an exchange of views between the law officers of the crown in Great Britain and the Department of Justice; and as a result, in 1924. I myself, as Minister of Justice, introduced a new resolution to this parliament with somew'hat different language. It was to the effect that	.
An enactment of the parliament of Canada, if expressed to operate extraterritorially, shall have, and be deemed to have had, that operation. if and in so far as it is a law for or ancillary to the peace, order and good government of Canada.
This resolution was voted by the parliament of Canada, but I may qualify this by saying that tlhe Senate amended it in some slight manner, so as to safeguard the rights of the provinces in that respect. The amendment came to the House of Commons on the last day of the session and was accepted then; but we found afterwards that the language was not exactly what it was intended to be, and that a new resolution would have to be passed by this house to amend it.
The whole question came before the Imperial conference of 1926, not brought there

Customs Act Amendment
by Canada but by other dominions, and it was then decided that this matter should be submitted as well as other matters to a committee of jurists which is to be appointed for the purpose of looking into all those questions. Meanwhile, as it is a very important matter concerning peace, order and good government in Canada, I think this parliament should take the same view as was taken in regard to the halibut fishery treaty, and that it should be made clear that as far as we are concerned we believe that for the peace, order and good government of Canada we should have in that respect the extraterritorial jurisdiction which the legislation of the Imperial parliament has provided with regard to their own affairs.

Mr. Chairman, I am veiy
much indebted to the minister, as I am sure the house is, for his discussion of the matter, and I can assure him that we are as desirous as hon. gentlemen opposite are to make effective and enforcible the customs laws of this country. Unfortunately I am not familiar with the section in the north Pacific convention to which he refers, and it is impossible without it before me to say whether it is the same as the proposed subsection 7 with which we are now dealing.
A number of the cases cited by the minister are not in point. For instance, the case of the ship North. The infraction in that case was committed within the teritorial jurisdiction of Canada, and what was involved was the right of immediate pursuit, or hot pursuit as it is termed. It seems to me we ought to approach this question frankly. The fact that the fishery decision was not challenged is no answer; that simply means that it has never stood the tect. What I have suggested, and what I suggest again, is that we should be frank in the matter. The Minister of Justice admits that there is doubt, and knowing that there is doubt, knowing that this provision is almost certain to be challenged, that seizures will be made within the twelve-mile limit, and that the question will come before the court and result in expensive litigation, why not go before the Imperial parliament and get legislation which will make it certain?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
My friend has not
noticed my statement in that respect. The Imperial government were quite willing to enact legislation to enforce the will of this parliament in that regard They asked, and we agreed, that the whole matter should come up with regard to the other dominions as well as to Canada. If Canada asks for that amendment, it will be made and agreed to by the Imperial parliament.

What I am suggesting is
that really the proper procedure would be to ask for it immediately, so that the customs laws can be enforced. There is grave doubt whether this is constitutional. My hon. friend is no doubt aware that Lord Halsbury has expressed the opinion that the colonies, including in that the self-governing dominions, have a jurisdiction which is territorial. What is going to be done in this case is tc create what amounts to a new and distinct criminal offence on the high seas, that is perhaps ten or twelve miles from the shore. The anomaly that will occur will be that you are creating the offence for Canadian vessels at a time when United States or French vessels can come inside and trade with impunity. As the minister is probably aware, the method adopted by the people engaged in this business to-day is to go to the West India island?, load up with a cargo usually consisting of rum, come to some prearranged point off the coast and there sell the cargo in the open sea. The law leaves the onus or responsibility of getting the goods, as they are called, on shore on the little man, not on the man who makes the purchase in the West Indies. The result will be simply that the business will be carried on by vessels other than those of Canadian registry and the section will be of no value.

If that be true, will it not be equally true, if we ask for the remedy that the hon. gentleman suggests, namely, that we secure an amendment to the British North America Act? Would that preclude United States vessels or vessels of any other country, from operating within the twelve-mile limit?

There are two points I want to make. I am suggesting first that this section is not constitutional and, second, even if it is enacted in this form, before you make treaty arrangements with other nations, you will not make any real headway in the suppression of smuggling. The result will be that vessels of Canadian registry will go to foreign ports, become registered there and carry on the business.

Is it not true that vessels
of Canadian ownership cannot obtain foreign registry?

It is very easy to make a
transfer which is only a transfer on paper. That is done every day.

This will at least make it
more difficult for them to do that.

It may. But I suggest that the difficulty will really amount to nothing in the final analysis. I started however on the
Customs Act Amendment

constitutional aspect of this sub-clause. I am suggesting that, as there is this grave doubt, and because, as the Minister of Justice has very frankly admitted, in face of all we have heard about the recent Imperial conference and Canada being a sovereign country, we are not really a sovereign country, we should go to the Imperial parliament and secure the necessary legislation.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
My hon. friend goes too far when he says that I admit that. I said that he was justified in expressing his views in that regard and he is not alone in holding that opinion, but I do not agree with him that this would be unconstitutional. I said that the bulk of authority is on the other side. May I quote one of our constitutional writers on the constitution of Canada, namely, Mr. Lefroy, who says:
Moreover, bearing in mind the fact that, as we shall see, the powers of the Dominion parliament, as also all the provincial legislatures are as plenary and ample within the limits prescribed by the British North America Act as the Imperial parliament in the plenitude of its power possessed and could bestow, and that the expressed intention was to confer upon the Dominion a constitution similar in principle to that of the United Kingdom, it seems beyond question that they must have the same power to bind their own subjects everywhere as the Imperial parliament has to bind British subjects everywhere.
A very distinguished legal gentleman, Sir John W. Salmond, who was Solicitor General of New Zealand, in an article in the Law Quarterly Review for 1917, writes as follows:
There is no rule of substantive constitutional law which prevents a colonial legislature from enacting such extraterritorial prohibitions or authorizations as may be required for the peace, order and good government of the colony.
Even the law officers of the crown in England, when this parliament adopted in 1920 the resolution to which I refer, make this statement in their correspondence with regard to air regulations, because it was on the matter of aviation that parliament was incited to ask that the whole matter should be cleared up because, as the committee will realize, it is very easy for an aviator to cross the boundary line and if parliament has no extraterritorial jurisdiction attached to its legislation, our law could be broken very easily. The law officers felt that the power actually possessed by the Dominion parliament entitled them to make their regulations applicable to Canadian aviators even for offences committed while they were outside of the boundaries of Canada. This question is being discussed in all the dominions. I remember that after the peace treaty, when the territory of Samoa was put under the mandate of New Zealand, New 
Zealand thought that as there was doubt as to her power of extraterritorial jurisdiction, she could not have her laws apply in that territory, and an imperial order in council was adopted for the purpose of giving that right to New Zealand. But General Smuts, who was then premier of South Africa, to which West Africa which had been taken from German}' was given as a mandatory territory, claimed that South Africa as a self-governing dominion had the right of extraterritoriality and no order in council or legislation was passed in order to give that additional right. So I think we are in pretty good company in asserting this right in this case and I am sure there will be no difficulty because the whole matter will be made clear when the judicial committee make a decision in this connection.

I cannot pretend to make
any legal argument and I have no intention of doing so, but I should like to set forth what I regard as a reasonable view to take of the situation. The department has been very much troubled by the practice of these rumsmuggling vessels loitering just beyond the three-mile limit and demoralizing the whole coast line in many instances.

They are not loitering
They are very active.

We want the power to cope with them just as quickly as possible. We might go to the British parliament and ask for an amendment to the British North America Act as the hon. member has suggested, but that would take time. There is, as the Minister of Justice has conceded, a reasonable doubt as to the constitutionality of what we propose to do, but there is a pretty strong presumption that we are right. If the clause goes through as it stands, we are certainly going to exercise our rights under it. Then we are in a practical position to have the constitutionality or legality of it tested out. The case will be fought out in the courts. If we win, the matter is settled. If we lose, we still have the remedy of going to the British parliament for an amendment to the British North America Act. We should like to have a remedy now. We are dealing with a difficult situation and if we postpone much longer dealing with it, it becomes all the more difficult to apply the remedy. I should also like to say in reply to my hon. friend when he spoke of the danger of our Canadian boats securing United States registry and becoming owned by Americans, that does not seem to me to be so serious a danger because of the fact-and I think I am right in this-that an American-owned vessel cannot legally carry liquor at all.

Customs Act Amendment
That is quite right.
But they do.

I hope the committee will
consent to leave the clause as it stands.

I am opposed to this
legislation for half a dozen reasons. In the first place, it is autocratic. In the next place, it will be inefficient, and I should think the minister by this time would have realized that. My hon. friend from Queens-Lunen-burg (Mr. Ernst) referred a moment ago to vessels going under American registry. I do not think they will go under American registry, but under Newfoundland or French registry, and what can the minister do then?
That would take some time.

It would take about fifteen minutes, just time enough for them to go down to St. Pierre, which is where the great bulk of this traffic originates, where it all originates so far as spirits are concerned. So far as ram is concerned, the traffic originates in the West Indies. The ships could also register in South America or British Honduras. There is no end of places where they could register.

They would have to change
ownership.

I can tell the minister
that they do not have to change ownership, and we have had abundant proof of that in the last two years in this house. That will not get you anywhere.
Then look at the provisions of this bill. Look at subsection 4, for instance. What is the effect of that? It is almost an inducement for his officers to commit murder and be held free of all consequences in doing so. That is a provision entirely uncalled for, and his proposals will be entirely ineffective. I think the minister himself is convinced of that fact, and if he is not, he ought to be. If he lived in the maritime provinces or in any maritime country he would realize what the difficulties are. You cannot stop rum running in that way. There is one simple method of stopping it to which I have referred before in this house several times, and that is by lowering the duty.
That will not stop it either.

It would stop 90 per
cent of it.

It will not stop it entirely
because smuggling existed before the duty was raised. I am not expressing any opinion whether the duty ought to be cut or not. I am rather in sympathy with what my hon.
friend suggests, but there was smuggling of liquor prior to the time that the duty was raised to 810 a gallon.

I am glad to have the
minister admit that he is in sympathy with my view. I knew that he was. Now why does he not act on that view? What is the use of our attempting to pass in this house legislation that we know we cannot enforce, and which is vicious in principle and contrary to British justice and contrary to all common-sense, because that is what it is. As I said before, you cannot stop smuggling in this way. I would ask the minister how much liquor was smuggled into Canada when the duty on whiskey was $1.80 a gallon? Smuggling was not worth while then, and it would not be done to-morrow under the same conditions, but the difficulty is that to-day on some of the liquor that is coming in the duty is practically 1,000 per cent. How are you going to stop smuggling under those conditions? The hon. member for Queens-Lun-enburg has referred to the modus operandi, how vessels come off the coast and peddle their goods to smaller boats that run them into the shore. The twelve mile limit will not affect these boats at all because they will be there under foreign registry. I am surprised that the Minister of Finance is supporting this legislation. He knows what the situation is, and he is the man who is responsible; there is no question about that, and I appeal to him and to the minister in charge of this bill to use that large stock of common-sense which I know they both possess and do what ought to be done instead of attempting in the way proposed by this bill to stop the smuggling of spirits.

I am sure that the reason for the amendment contained in subsection 7 is because the minister feels that extending our territorial waters to the twelve mile limit will have a greater effect in stopping smuggling than when the territorial waters extend only to the three mile limit. That may be quite true. But if it is true, I would like to ask the minister why he has increased the limit from three miles only to twelve miles, because if the twelve mile limit is going to be more effectual than the three mile limit in preventing smuggling, and if this parliament has the power to extend the limit. I respectfully submit that instead of making the limit twelve miles the minister should make it fifty miles, because then the vessels would have to lay off fifty miles from the shore, and if they oa.me within the fifty miles the revenue cutters of the minister would be able to seize them and take them into port and
Customs Act Amendment

tie them up. This is a good subsection if this parliament has the constitutional power to enact it, which I very much doubt. I agree with the hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg that this is an international matter; it is not a matter for the British parliament at all The worst feature of this legislation is that the ships of Great Britain, where they manufacture the whiskey, can load up with whiskey in Scotland and then come across and lay to off the United States and our Canadian coast, while our own ships will have to lay to beyond the twelve mile limit. If the British government was so anxious to stop the smuggling of whiskey into Canada, they should agree not to allow their own vessels to clear from their own ports when they know that they are going to break the laws of Canada. But 'if we have the constitutional right to enact a subsection of this kind, which I very much doubt, then let the minister go the whole way and instead of making the limit twelve miles, make it perhaps fifty miles. I would ask the minister why he fixed upon twelve miles rather than some other figure.

I suppose it really springs
from a recommendation based upon the limit which they have along the coast of the United States. I have no constitutional objection to making it fifteen or twenty miles. As a matter of fact, I think it was eighteen miles in the first draft, but we reduced it to twelve to conform, I suppose, with the case I have cited. That is all; there is no other reason. Fifty miles might sound a little unreasonable.

The results on the United
States coast have not been very successful, and I think we should go them one better, and if the minister would agree, I would ask him to amend his bill to make the limit twenty-five or fifty miles instead of twelve.
I think we had better try the half of it first.
I am suggesting fifty.
Why not send your cutters right down to St. Pierre and seize these boats just as soon as they come out of port with a full cargo? That shows the ridiculousness of the position the minister takes.

Section agreed to.
Section 2 agreed to.
On section 3-vessel carrying dutiable or prohibited goods liable to seizure.

I think this section needs careful examination on the part of the minister. May I point out to him the exact wording of it? By subsection 7 of section 1 we

have in so far as Canadian vessels are concerned extended, prima facie at least, the territorial waters of Canada to twelve miles from the shore. Now section 3 reads:
If upon the examination by any officer of the cargo of any vessel hovering in territorial waters of Canada-
Let us say that she is eleven and three-quarter miles from the shore:
-any dutiable goods or any goods the importation of which into Canada is prohibited are found on board, such vessel .... shall be forfeited.
I quite appreciate why that provision should be made in the case of alcoholic liquors, but in the case of other goods a vesel can scarcely be within the territorial waters of Canada or anywhere else without having some dutiable goods on board. If she has dutiable goods of any character, no matter where they may come from, and she is found in the territorial waters of Canada within the twelve-mile limit-
She must be hovering.

Let us say that she had to
heave to because of stress of weather, the question arises whether or not she is hovering, and she may be seized unjustifiably. Why not limit the clause to alcoholic liquors?
I think the preventive forces will have to be given credit for exercising reasonable discretion in these matters. In my opinion we ought not to make the distinction my hon. friend suggests.

I would cite another case to the minister. A yacht is cruising, your officers may term it hovering within the twelve-mile limit; she has an admiralty warrant, which gives her the right to take out of bond liquor and other dutiable goods; she has these goods on board legally-they are not dutiable; a revenue cutter overhauls the yacht, and according to this section she may be seized and condemned. What is to be done in that case?

That would not be cargo at
all, but ships' stores.

The section says that if
dutiable or other goods are found on board the vessel ihall be seized and forfeited.

I agree with the hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg (Mr. Ernst) that fishing vessels sometimes anchor off the Nova Scotia coast to pursue their peaceful avocation of catching cod and haddock. Under this section the preventive officers may go aboard, demand the ship's papers, and make a search.

That is an extreme case.
Her clearance papers disclose her status, and if she is engaged in that pursuit the preventive officers cannot accuse her of hovering.

Section agreed to.
Sections 4, 5 and 6 agreed to.
On section 7-Export of deer.

What changes are made
in the regulations with respect to the export of deer?

Under the present law citizens of Canada are not permitted, for instance, to export deer hides. It very often happens that there is no market for them in Canada but there is in the United States.

maintopic: LOAN OF $500,000,000 REDEMPTION OF LOANS AND PURCHASE OF UNMATURED SECURITIES
speechtext:
The minister has not given us any information as to how he proposes to utilize this money. Conferring upon the governor in council power to borrow half a billion dollars for the purpose of redeeming existing securities is a very large grant of power without any scheme being submitted.
I had occasion a few days ago to draw attention to the course pursued in England. Whenever it is contemplated by legislation there to retire existing securities, it has always been the custom to formulate a plan, and when the house is in committee the Chancellor of the Exchequer expounds at length the principles which govern in connection with the redemption of outstanding securities or the conversion of existing loans. Now this measure contemplates the possibility of conversion; that is clear. It must mean that. It contemplates the possibility of borrowing $500,000,000, let us say, at 4 per cent for the purpose of retiring existing securities, if they were selling at such a rate as would enable the minister to make money thereby. That is clearly what he has in mind. Sir HENRY" DRAYTON: My hon. friend is right, and yet perhaps he is wrong. It is not quite fair to say that the government borrow7 on the same security used by the banks; they do not. As a rule the government gives its obligation with no further security, and that is first rate security. When the banks come to the Department of Finance for a loan, they do not give their obligations or anything like that; they give securities in other forms. For instance, when we had the stress on the currency at the time we first stopped the operations of the wheat
[Mr. Bnbb.l

My hon. friend from Battle River (Mr. Spencer) has followed this question very carefully, and he will recall the evidence given before the committee on banking and commerce the other day by Mr. Harding, who pointed out that all these emissions of currency, or emissions of credit one way or the other, have to be controlled by something which would make for an immediate and proper return at the right time, in order to do away with any danger of inflation. All these bank transactions are protected and fortified in that way. For example, when we looked after the financing of the wheat crop, all the emissions at that time which were on a 5 per cent basis, all the extra currency, all the issues had to be retired, because it was manifestly in the interests of the banks to retire them as soon as possible.

The treasury report fixes the rate of interest, at least it ought to fix its rate of interest having regard to the then value of money and the then needs of Canadian commerce. My own view is that the latter consideration is greater than the first, but those are the two great considerations one must always have in mind. speechtext:
The minister ought to
know his department by this time, having been in it for several years.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: How long?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
If hon. members on that side have not anyone who can master it in a few months, I can pick out a dozen over here who could do so.
In the first place, Mr. Chairman, I object to the soldiers' department being wiped out. I am not averse to creating a department that will be wholly concerned with the returned soldiers. You have your land settlement scheme, which the government have very conveniently dropped so far as the soldiers are concerned, but which I think ought to be revived in the interest of this country. Then again, those of us who have been sitting on the pension committee know that there are innumerable problems coming up all the time. Our advice from the officials appearing before that committee is that these problems are going to increase, and at the very moment when they are on the verge of increasing and giving us a lot of difficulty, the whole soldiers' department is to be wiped out.
Pensions and National Health

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
No.
Mr. MeGIBBON:	I say it is wiped out.
It is fundamentally changed and absorbed into another department. That is obvious from the very fact that you are putting the soldiers' department under another deputy minister who will be the executive head. The minister is making a mistake, and so far as I am concerned I am going to oppose the change.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: This bill might well be called the narcotic bill, because it is intended to put to sleep, if not put out of business, the soldiers' department. Personally I object to an amalgamation which makes the soldiers' department subordinate to any other department. I do not care how many departments you tack on to the soldiers' department, but I object to making it secondary to any other. I have no objection to the deputy minister of health being made the deputy minister of the soldiers' department, because he is a good man with considerable experience, and perhaps there is no one better qualified. Secondly, I object to the name, "national health and soldiers' welfare". That smacks too much of the child welfare movement, and suggests that it is just about of the same importance. The minister has failed to give us any reasons for this amalgamation. Would he tell us, to begin with, of any one section of the Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment Department that is being wiped out? Perhaps the one nearest to it would be the workshops, but if the minister had been in the committee this morning he would have come to the conclusion that there is more necessity for the workshops movement to-day than ever before.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
I am familiar
with that.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
The minister also
says that there may be changes in the financing and accounting systems. Has the Department of Health any branch that can do that work? Then in connection with the work of re-establishment-

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
My hon. friend
is under a misapprehension. I stated very definitely the other night that this section would remain distinct, and operate on the lines along which has hitherto proceeded.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
Then why not leave it alone? I do not care how many departments you amalgamate with the Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment, but what we do object to is that this important department should be tacked on to the Department of Health. The Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment Depart-
TMr. McGibbon.]
ment is more important than the Department of Health, and if the minister would consider it in that light perhaps there would not be as much objection. What does the minister expect to accomplish in the way of economy and efficiency by wiping out the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-estaiblishment? I do not care for the report of Mr. Scott or anyone else; we all recognize the fact that changes could be made. Put Mr. Scott in any other department of government and he might well make a similar report. What benefits or economies will be effected by this change?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
My hon. friend was informed a few moments ago that considerable economy had already been effected in the internal organization of the Ottawa branch by centralizing our auditing, registration and accounting systems. That will be evident when my estimates are before the house, for I shall then move for their reduction. The reorganization beyond the central department has not yet been completed. It will be carried out by officers of the department after careful investigation. The suggestion that the organization which has been dealing with the soldiers' affairs will be wiped out is not fair and cannot be attributed to anything that I have said; in fact my remarks have all been to the contrary; and there is very littlle use in trying to create that impression. For many years to come we know there will have to be an organization to deal with the problems to which my hon. friend from Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. Clark) referred. They are soldier problems.
As to the proposed amalgamation, I have quoted authorities from my hon. friends opposite in support of it. Only two or three years ago the then leader of the Conservative party intimated that the department should be done away with, and there have been other suggestions from all sides of the house that it might well be amalgamated with another department. My observations convinced me of the wisdom of this course, and my judgment has since been confirmed by an independent audit.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
I do not think the minister has added to our information; all he says is that the registration office and another section will be combined. That is no argument for the proposed amalgamation. Two or three years ago I suggested that the department itself might well consolidate two or three of its sections; but I cannot understand why the soldiers' department should be placed under the Health department in order to bring together a couple of sections within the department, itself. I still think that the amalgamation is all right in principle, but I

Pensions and National Health
fail to see any reason for putting the Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment department under the Health department. The minister's idea was that a rose by any other name would smell as sweet. Well, whether you call it a rose, a leek, or any other name, I would remind the minister that something goes along with the name. The mere fact that two or three members who are not returned men made certain suggestions does not necessarily make those suggestions of any greater value than if they proceeded from returned men. I think any returned man will say that the proposed title is destructive of the idea of sympathy which we all entertain for our returned soldiers.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Probably the apprehensions of my hon. friends are due to the fact that they are still discussing the title of the amalgamated department. As I understand, my colleague has already moved an amendment to the resolution whereby the name is to be left over for further consideration.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
We are not objecting
to that.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
At the same time I feel
sure that he and his friends have that in the back of their heads, if they will permit me to say so. This must be so when it is suggested that the veterans' department is to be wiped out, because the resolution does not so provide.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
The minister himself
admitted that it is to be put under the Health department.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
I beg my hon. friend's
pardon; nobody has admitted anything of the kind. The resolution provides that there is to be an amalgamation of the two departments. The Department of Health happens to be mentioned first. If the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment had been mentioned first, I suppose my hon. friend would have claimed that it was swallowing up the Department of Health. As I understand it, the activities of the Health department will carry on, and the activities of the department which was known as the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment

which perhaps is no longer an accurate title-will also carry on. According to the report submitted to the hon. minister, there will be a saving of administration expenses, and he has already intimated that his estimates will show a reduction. So far as economy is concerned, it seems to me that that ought to satisfy my hon. friends, for the present at least.
The two departments are made into one, but, I repeat, the veterans' department is not
to be wiped out. So far as I am concerned, I am perfectly happy to have the names of the departments reversed, so that the soldier activities should be mentioned first in the title and the health activities second. One or the other must be mentioned first; you cannot mention both in the same breath. I think such a change should at least remove the objection that the soldiers' department will be wiped out. While listening to the discussion it seemed to me that the title Department of Pensions and Health would meet all the objections which have been made on this score. In England the department which administers soldiers' affairs is called the Ministry of Pensions. Someone may say that that does not include treatment. Biit the point is that treatment is only ancillary to pensions. You treat a man in hospital in order that he may be cured of his disability so far as possible and his pension reduced if he gets into a better physical state. Therefore I think the word "pensions" will cover the general activities in regard to ex-service men.
I disagree with my hon. friend from Van-couver-Burrard-with whom I am generally in accord on soldier matters-in suggesting that the word "soldiers" be retained. I do not think the ex-service man wants to be still regarded as a soldier. The department over which I happen to preside has to do with soldier matters, and it seems to me there will be some difficulty in the public mind if you have two departments, both apparently having to do with military affairs. The word " re-establishment " is also equally inappropriate in view of the fact that re-establishment in so far as it refers to land settlement, vocational training and so on, has been largely done away with. Therefore I think the time is come when the department may well be called by the name which best expresses its activities- the Department of Pensions. Whether the title be the Department of Health and Pensions, the Department of National Health and Pensions, or the Department of Pensions and National Health. I do not think makes the least difference. The ex-service man will not be very much concerned with the discussion we are now having as to the title of the amalgamated department; he wants to be assured that his difficulties and problems will be squarely faced; and the minister assures us that will be done. I think hon. gentlemen who have listened to the evidence which has been given before the special committee this session have realized that the officials of the department are alive to the interests of the ex-service men, and are endeavouring to do their duty in that respect. These officials will
Pensions and National Health

be the officials of the pension side of the new department and will proceed to carry on in the same way. Let us get out of our minds the obsession in regard to the name, and realize that we are dealing with a resolution that contemplates the amalgamation of two departments, preserving the activities of both but under one head. After all, it is just the same as it was previously, because my hon. friend has been minister of both departments and there is no difference m administration. It seems to me that we shall be able to think a little more clearly-if I may say this without offence-and get along with the real question in hand if we do not concentrate so much on the name. The important thing is what will be involved in the matters that will come up as a result of the report of the committee.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Will there be two deputies or one?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: One.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Let us disabuse our minds of the idea that the soldiers department will be wiped out. I do not think my hon. friends want to be unfair, nor do they want the country to get any such impression. I believe that if they will read the resolution carefully, and listen to the explanation of the minister, they will offer no objection, because nothing is further from the fact than the thought that the activities now carried on in the interests of the ex-service men will be abandoned or in any way curtailed. I do not want to review the matter to-day; some time I may do so. But the activities of the past four or five years, and the legislation that has been passed in that time, will convince this committee and the country, I think, that there has been a real appreciation of the problems of the soldiers and an endeavour to improve in every possible way by legislation the situation as we have it.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
The minister mentioned a short time ago, in connection with the question of names, that my suggestion was. "national health and veterans' affairs". The suggestion which I made at the inception of this discussion was "soldiers' affairs", but the Minister of National Defence has rather convinced me that "soldiers' affairs" would be better replaced by "veterans' affairs", in view of the fact that his department also covers soldier activities in the sense of dealing with men in active service at the present time. I suggest therefore that the name should be the "Department of Veterans' Affairs and National Health". I think that veterans' affairs should come first: it is veterans' matters with which we are dealing, as the Min-
[Mr. Ralston.!
ister of National Defence has pointed out. The question of national health should come second. I agree with the Minister of Health that the word "national" has a place. Some of my colleagues here have considered it wise inasmuch as there are departments of agriculture and of health in the provinces. The only purpose of and advantage in using the word "national" in this connection is that it would be a clear indication to people at large that this was a federal department. Some years ago in Vancouver there was a soldier settlement board and a department of the provincial government-I have forgoten its exact designation-with a similar name, and this made for some confusion.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Land settlement.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: My suggestion is, therefore, that the title should be "Department of Veterans' Affairs and National Health".

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
It has been my experience
in this house over many years that nothing is so pleasant as the announcement that some department will be amalgamated with another, while there is nothing the house dreads so much as the creation of a new department. It is an old standing grievance that we have too many departments, and I have heard many complaints from both political parties on that score, accordingly as they sat to the right or to the left of the Speaker. The argument has been always the same. So far as the soldiers are concerned, they objected strenuously' not long ago to being linked up with the Department of National Defence, on the ground that they were no longer soldiers and wished therefore to be treated as civilians. Now there is something in having a brief name for the departmeni ; a long name is quite unnecessary. It strikes me that if the word " welfare " is going to be retained the title of the department should be simple and brief:	" Department of
National Welfare". I suggest this in view of the fact that the departments of Customs and Excise have been called the Department of National Revenue. If you are going to call it the department of health and veterans, very well; but why add the word "welfare"? If you want to summarize the name, make it as brief as possible and call it the Department of National Welfare.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
Will you please
translate that into French so that we may see what it looks like?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
It would be "Le departernent du Bien-etre national". There is nothing to be gained by having a long name for

Pensions and National Health
the department. The suggestion of the Minister of National Defence, of "Pensions and Health", might also be recommended on the ground intimated, that the name of a department .should indicate its activities as far as possible.
I think the government should be congratulated on the attempt which is being made to amalgamate our departments so far as this is deemed wise, because the cost of civil government in this country has been increasing at an enormous rate. If hon. members want to get an idea of what government now costs, they should go back to the estimates that used to be presented in this house thirty years ago. That would open their eyes, and I do not think, in the light of the comparison, that they would object to this amalgamation. If dollars are to be saved the country by this amalgamation, efficiency being promoted at the same time, the proposal should receive the support of the house. Economy is particularly necessary in the administration of the affairs of the country at this time owing to the enormous burdens we have to bear and the great problems we have to face.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
I am glad to hear one
voice in the wilderness over there preaching economy; it is the first one I have heard this session from that side. In reply to the Minister of National Defence I wish to say this: my objection is not to the name at all; I have tried to make that clear. I object to the soldiers' department being united with the Department of Health in any shape or form.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Would you object to the Department of Health being united to the soldiers' department?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
Yes, equally. I claim
there are soldier problems enough in this country to justify retaining the department. You might combine pensions, land settlement and soldier problems, which we are discussing every day in the committee. We were told oniy this morning in the committee that there were 2,000 problems cases before the country to-day, registered, and the opinion was that these did not constitute any large percentage of the total. They did not think for a moment that the cases were all registered.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Those are pension cases.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
They are problem cases, including both pensions and other matters. They are problem cases which the department must look after, and everyone knows that they will increase as the days go by. Now
what are you doing? You are taking the deputy minister from the Department of Health and putting him in charge of the whole thing. He is to be the business head, notwithstanding that he has never been associated for a moment with the soldiers' department. Ten years after the war you are taking the head of some department other than that concerned with the soldiers and putting him over the amalgamated department?. Your deputy minister should be one who has been in touch with these problems all along. Surely there are in the present department men who have been in touch right along with these soldier problems, with seven or eight years' experience behind them. Then there is the pensions committee, with all its ramifications; and you have the soldier land settlement board, which could be brought under; it deals with soldier problems.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
My hon. friend does not
want any more brought in?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
I presume the theory
is that the department has not enough work. If you amalgamate all the soldier activities there will be plenty of work, and I think there is plenty now.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Would the veterans like to be linked up with the Department of National Defence as far as pensions are concerned? I think they would strenuously object.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: I was not discussing the Department of National Defence.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: I understood the hon. member to say he wanted all soldier activities under the Department of National Defence.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
I was refering to returned soldiers' problems, and I think these problems are going to increase and become more acute as the years go by. There is bound to be some interlocking between the work of these different departments such as the Pension board and the present Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment, and this interlocking will become more apparent in the future. Problems will come up then which we do not face now; disabilities will increase as the men get older, and as I have already said in this house there are a large number of additional diseases breaking out. A regular wave of insanity is sweeping over this country which everyone knows is the result of w'ar service but which cannot be definitely connected up with it. That, is a problem which is bound to become more acute, and I believe there is plenty of work in all the departments dealing with returned soldiers to keep the deputy minister and his staff busy. I do object to
Pensions and National Health

having this work united with the work of the Department of Health; I think it needs a live organization and a deputy minister who has been connected with it for the past ten years.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
I had not intended to take
part in the discussion of the principle of this matter, because I do not think it is of very much importance to the returned soldier by what name the department is called. Personally I do not care what they call it so long as they keep on giving the service they have given for the past few years. However, I cannot believe that the hon. member (Mr. McGibbon) really understands the purpose of this bill. He has been telling us that he objects to having the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment tacked on to the Department of Health.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Or vice versa.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: He does not want the Department of Health to have anything to do with the Department of Soldiers' Civil Reestablishment; but surely he knows that the two departments have been under the one head for eight years or more. The objection of the hon. member, therefore, must be to the deputy, but I am sure he must be aware that the present deputy minister of health, who will be the executive head of the amalgamated departments, is Doctor Amyot, who had a magnificent war record overseas and who among all our physicians who served in France was particularly distinguished. So he is well aware of the problems of the returned soldier. If we should have a returned soldier as deputy minister of this department I submit that he should be a medical man as well, who can look on all these questions from both points of view.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
I am not criticizing
Doctor Amyot in the least, but does my hon. friend know the position he occupied overseas?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
I am not quite sure, but I
believe he was either an A.D.M.S. or a D.D.M.S.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
He was engaged in
sanitation work.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: I know he had a high executive position. He may have been dealing with sanitation also, but if the hon. member wishes me to do so I will look up his record, or will ask the minister to do so.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Oh, no.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
So the only objection we have had so far is that these two departments are to have the same deputy minister, but

the hon. member must be aware of the fact that all the higher officials of the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment are to remain in that department.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: I do not like to interrupt, but my point is that we should have a deputy who has been conversant with this work for at least the last ten years.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
I have no doubt that the next deputy minister of that department wili be someone who has been conversant with the work for ten years, but at present that position is vacant, and in order to fill it a new man would have to be appointed. In that case a man would have to be taken from the Department of Soldiers' Civil Reestablishment, which doubtless would meet with some objection from hon. members opposite who have constantly criticized that department; or we would have to take an outside man with no experience. If we must take an outside man I see no reason why we should not take a soldier with a distinguished overseas record, who knows something of medical matters as well.
The suggestion has been made by the minister that the bill based upon this resolution should be referred to the committee dealing with pensions and returned soldier problems, and to that suggestion I wish to object most strenuously. I have no desire to exaggerate the amount of work which is before that committee at present, but we have been sitting almost every day since the opening of the session. We have heard innumerable witnesses; the evidence we have heard covers some 800 or 900 pages, which we have to wade through before we can make a report. We have had suggestions and submissions with regard to pensions, and I also happen to have with me a list of the subjects which have been brought before this committee. They are as follows: Pensions; civil service preference; employment of returned soldiers; grave markers; returned soldiers' insurance; last post fund; medical examination and treatment; returned soldiers' advisers; old age pensions; Victoria Cross veterans; housing schemes; indigent veterans; soldier settlement boards; vetcraft shops, and recently the Minister of National Defence referred to this committee a bill dealing with canteen funds.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Does not the hon. member think that is enough work for one department?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
I am quite sure it is enough for one department, but it would not hurt to add the little work which the doctors of this country would give. We have all that work before the committee, and although I

Pensions and National Health
do not wish to make that work appear unduly important lest when the report is brought down someone may say, "Parturiunt montes, nascetur ridiculus mus", I think we have enough work to keep us busy until the end of the session. There is this further point, that hitherto in this house matters relating to returned soldiers such as pensions and so on have been dealt with in an impartial, nonpartisan manner. It has been shown clearly that this question of amalgamation is a matter of government policy; perhaps otherwise there would not be so much opposition to it. If a matter of government policy is brought before this committee it is likely to be opposed or upheld on grounds not unconnected with political partisanship, and I believe it very important that the discussion of matters which relate to the welfare of our returned soldiers should be free from even a suspicion of partisanship. I therefore ask the members of the house not to refer this bill or any question arising out of it to the committee on pensions and returned soldiers problems.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
I certainly agree with the
member for Quebec South (Mr. Power) that the committee which is at present sitting is loaded with work; and I should like also at this moment to pay a tribute to the work of the chairman of that committee, who has been there daily and has been indefatigable in his efforts. It struck me when he read the list 'of matters which are being dealt with by that committee that there must be work for at least one department; and it also struck me that perhaps there is nothing so important as the organization of that department. I am not so sure that the committee which is now sitting is not perhaps the best qualified of all the bodies at present functioning to give consideration to the method and manner of organization of this particular department.
As I have said before, and I have said it repeatedly, I am not quibbing over a name; but I want to be convinced that there is going to be some increased efficiency and some real economy. I have not heard anything which would give any indication of that, except the minister's statement that when the estimates comes up he will move for a reduction; but he does not give us any idea of what will be the nature or extent of that measure of economy. The Minister of National Defence said that things would be just as they are-I think I am quoting him correctly-[DOT]

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
That the same service
will be carried on.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
Then I would say if they
are going to be just as they are, the only
thing we are doing here is to change the name; and if that is the only job we have it seems to me we are wasting a lot of time. We might just as well-

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Will my hon. friend permit me? When I said that, I called attention to the statement which had been made by the minister with regard to the reduction, and also the report as to the saving in administration expenses.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
I mentioned that, and I
say that is the only reason, so far as I can see, which has been given for the change. But there has been no indication as to what those reductions will be, what will be the saving, and what will be the increased efficiency. If they are to be just as they are,
I conceive that the department is going_ to operate with the organization as it exists, and there would be very little advantage except that there will be one deputy minister instead of two; and there has been one minister for the past eight years, as has been indicated. The only change, so far as I can observe, is one deputy minister instead of two. Well, there is some economy, I suppose; but the member for Quebec South has stated there is a tremendous number of problems to be dealt with; and the question is can they be dealt with efficiently by one deputy head? Judging from the amount of work which this committee has before it, I question whether it can be done efficiently. We would like some conclusive evidence that there is to be increased efficiency, something more than a mere change to one deputy head where there were two, and something more than the mere change of name.
So far as the name is concerned, some names have been mentioned to which I do object so much, though I do net consider the name of any great importance. The name the minister suggested is simple and I think applicable, and so far as I am concerned personally I would be prepared to support it. I do not see, however, wrhy he should object to 11 soldier problems" or "soldier reestablishment ". Every man who served is known as a returned soldier and is proud of it; he speaks of himself as a returned soldier and will be known and will speak of himself as such until the day he dies. So that I think the words " returned soldier " will always be in use when we are speaking of the men who served during the great war.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
My objection to the explanation given by the minister has been that apparently he is subordinating soldier services to that of health. I submit that the name he announced and the explanation he offered left
Pensions and National Health

that impression upon me and upon others, particularly on this side of the house, and will undoubtedly leave that impression throughout the country. Without criticizing the minister, I would point out that naturally the minister looks at these matters of health as the most, important as between the two departments. All the explanations he has given have rather confirmed me in the idea that the first element in this whole question as it presents itself to his mind is that of what he calls national health. Now, I submit that that is not the important thing. The important thing is to look after our soldiers. The problems in connection with returned soldiers are getting more complex as the years go on. I think all will admit that. I know many cases in my own county which have developed within the last two or three years, and have developed in a way and in numbers and of a character that I fancy was not contemplated by anybody three or four or five years ago. I am sure the Minister of National Defence will agree that that is by far the most important side of what is proposed to be combined under one department. I am afraid that the minister (Mr. King, Kootenay) does not realize that, and is not in full sympathy with that side of the question.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
My hon. friend
should not say that. It is not a fair statement-that I am not in sympathy.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
Possibly I did not make myself sufficiently clear. What I wished to point out is this, that I think his first love is with the medical side. I am not at all blaming him for that. Consciously or unconsciously, I think that would be true, and I am not blaming him for it. I may be wrong, but he is a medical man, and I think that is the part of the combined department which would appeal most to him. speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, although not myself a returned soldier, I have been closely associated with their affairs during the past few years, and from my point of view the proposed change may be beneficial in its effects. We have heard a good deal uf criticism as to the cost of administration of the department as compared with the money actually paid to the men themselves. The opinion has been expressed that too great a proportion of the vote has been spent in administrative costs. This change, if carried out properly, will I think reduce that proportion; it will enable us to decrease the appropriation to some extent without affecting adversely the returned men. In other words it will increase the amount spent directly for the benefit of the returned men and decrease the expenditure for administrative purposes. So far I think the change is well warranted and will have beneficial results.
There are one or two dangers to be guarded against. The first is that the department of soldiers' affairs, or whatever it may be called, should be made subordinate or minimized by the amalgamation. It is our opinion in this corner; it is my opinion very strongly that that will be the heaviest and most important end of the work for a long time to come; that the greatest stress will have to be placed upon that work, and that anything which would minimize the importance of that work should be deprecated. But I fail to see that an amalgamation, if properly organized and carried out, would have that effect. If an amalgamation is to take place, I can conceive of no more proper department for the amalgamation than that of Health, because a great deal of the work in connection with soldiers' problems deals with medical examination, or in other words with health. The basis of all the assistance which we are obliged tc give, the basis of all the pensions which are earned is the question of health and physical disability and the question of medical opinion, and if there is one department more than another which could be attached to the department of soldiers' affairs it would rightly be that of Health. I am- not sufficiently well acquainted with the internal economy of the two departments to be able to say what the saving would be; but I believe it might be of such an amount as to be well worthy of consideration, and I am prepared to support the amalgamation as long as it is apparent, through

Pensions and National Health
the bill which will present the details of that amalgamation, that the necessities and problems of the returned men will be kept to the front and will not in any way be ignored or minimized.
As regards the name, I must confess that I am not very much interested except to this extent: once we adopt the principle that the department of soldiers' affairs, or problems, or whatever you like to call it, is the important end of the work, the name should advertise that principle to the country so that there will be, in the minds of the returned men themselves, no misconception as to the amalgamation. That is why I attach importance to the name-not because the name itself will make any difference to the work done, but because of the moral effect of the name upon the men affected. As so many names have been already suggested I am not going to suggest another. Granting those two premises, first, that the soldiers' problems will be kept to the front; that their importance will be recognized; that the growing importance and scope of the problems will be realized; second, that, the organization will be of such a character that that work will come first, and third, if I may add another, that the name decided upon will be one which will give to the country and the returned men the proper impression of the amalgamation which is to be effected, I am prepared to support the amalgamation.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I can hardly take that in. Navigation is paramount.

Navigation is paramount, but my friend the minister overlooks this fact, that parliament has control over navigation; it can impede navigation, and sometimes has done so; and navigation is not paramount unless this parliament keeps it paramount. It may or may not be paramount, depending upon what the attitude of this parliament may be. Leaving that aside for a moment, we will assume that parliament has concluded that the bridge company shall exist? Now what is the result? We have given, as the books say, life and vitality to something, an entity that we hereafter call the bridge company or whatever it may be; it comes into being by act of this parliament; it is clothed with the power that this parliament confers upon it. Leaving out for a moment the question of the power to construct the bridge, let. us say that the view suggested by the Minister of the Interior is sound, that the project is subject to the provisions of the Navigable Waters Act and that there must be the consent of the minister. In this bill the governor in council must consent before it comes into force.

Now come to the next point. It is a toll bridge, is it not? Last week the governor of New York state vetoed all bridge bills dealing with tolls, declaring that the time had come in his country when the state can borrow money so much more cheaply than the individual that if it is desirable to construct bridges over any water on which people shall be charged tolls, that the people should pay the least possible toll; which means that the public should build the bridge and recoup themselves from the tolls. That is the position which the governor took. Is not that a sound principle?
The government must adopt some principle in regard to this. Is it the sound principle that the capitalists of any country shall meet together, form themselves into a syndicate and then take this company's charter, which gives them a living entity called the St. Clair Transit Company, charge tolls to yield back to them the cost of this bridge and interest on their money, with all the promotion expenses incidental to it, with the stock issued under the terms mentioned in the bill; then say that they shall have these powers conferred upon them, and when they get their money back that the bridge shall revert to certain people? If it is in the public interest, that a bridge be built at St. Clair let the people of this country give their collective credit to it, and the country will get the money much cheaper than anybody else can get it. We have had a number of toll bridges in this country, but they have been abolished in most of the provinces because it has been found a most unfair use of the powers of parliament to create them; and I think the last one was brought out in the older provinces. I cannot speak of them all, but I know that has been done.
