What relation the services rendered have to the stock issued has been settled by a series of cases. We had one in the Supreme Court of Canada in which the whole of the capital stock of the company was issued not for services but-
For a boat, a one-man company?

No, not for a boat. It was one of the Orchard cases, and the court said it will not be astute to discover whether the consideration is adequate up to a single dollar, but whether it bears some relation to the capital stock issued for it. The minister will probably bear that case in mind. I sent for Palmer's Company Precedents, but I did 56103-129
not get them in time to turn up the section from which this is taken, because I imagine, with certain changes, this is the form which will be found in Palmer's Company Precedents.
I thought I recognized it too. But is the hon. member sure that paragraph (b) is in the English statutes?

That was my memory
when I read it.
I have Lindley's Company Law here.

My hon. friend will remember that the Companies' Act was amended, but I do not think Lindley's to which he refers deals with the latest amendments to the Companies' Act. The paragraph to which the Minister of Railways takes exception is one that can have no effect at all upon the question now before the house. It is a paragraph that becomes operative only in event of the company failing to discharge their duties. In other words, if they take the chance of issuing shares without fulfilling the agreement called for by the preceding sub-paragraphs, then they run the risk of being liable for the par value of the shares. But in this case the difficulty is that no par value is attached to the shares. That is an unusual feature with respect to the matter. Furthermore, the Minister of Railways was very fearful lest this should result in litigation. Let me point out to him that the courts, rightly or wrongly, decided two generations ago that any man who buys shares in a company must be considered as having read the memorandum and the articles of association. He buys them at his peril and when he buys shares in this enterprise he knows that that paragraph is there. The courts decided that question very early in the history of incorporated companies. There having been fixed upon him the onus of knowing what he is buying, the terms of this section are known to him, and if he buys shares, like a pig-in-a-poke, without knowing what he is buying, the law says that that is his business, because it attributes to him, when he bought the diares, knowledge of the charter and all its terms. That is the position with respect to that.
The matter has nothing more than a general public interest so far as I am concerned but this is a step backwards in the worst sense. No such legislation as this would be passed in these days by any parliament or legislature that I know of. It would be desired by promoters if they could secure it. It has about it all the earmarks of legislation that existed in the United States at least fifty years ago and about which we read so much, except that

SI. Clair Transit Company

it has set no par value for the shares instead of setting a par value of a fixed price per share. It does permit, in its very terms, of the issue of shares for the service of getting this charter through the House of Commons, the expense of preparing the bill and other expenses incidental to the completion of the charter.
The government should have a well-defined policy with respect to this bridge, indeed with respect to all these bridges. The government should have enunciated a policy with respect to all these bridges that cross international waterways. It is neither meet nor proper nor just nor in the public interest of this country that private bills should be introduced and passed through parliament because someone is rather a nice gentleman, you like him, you do not like to vote against him, you have a desire to accommodate him and a desire to support his bill. It is not a pleasant thing to vote against legislation promoted by my hon. friend whose name is on this bill; anyone would like to oblige him by voting in supfport of his bill, and too often the public interest is subordinated to our personal likes or dislikes and the popularity or unpopularity of the person who has the legislation in charge. I have discharged my duty in the matter of directing the attention of the administration to these facts, to the abuses that will follow and to the retrograde character of the legislation, which is at variance with all modem ideas. The time has come for the enunciation and declaration of a policy in regard to bridges crossing international waters instead of leaving such bills in the hands of a private member who, by suggesting that if you and your friends will support my bill, I and my friends will support yours, may be able to get it through the select standing committee and into the House of Commons and then, with the aid of party associations and good friendship, get it through the house. I will vote for the amendment as a protest against legislation of this character and I leave with the government the responsibility of having placed upon the statute books of this country legislation which is more backward in its character and more far-reaching in its effects than any bills of a similar nature to which my attention has been directed in recent times.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. L. RALSTON (Minister of National Defence):
speechtext:
Just two points. At first I was
impressed by what was said by the mover of the amendment with regard to this being copied from the English statutes. Is that correct?
The principle, I mean.

My hon. friend is wrong
about that, as I felt sure he was. There is a principle which is contained in a good many of the provincial companies' acts and that principle is that when shares are issued for a consideration other than cash, the contract showing the consideration for those shares shall be filed with the registrar of joint stock companies in order that anyone who buys shares may have an opportunity of going to the registrar's office and seeing just exactly what property the shares represent. In other words it provides publicity in order that a man may see just what he is buying when he buys these shares. That provision was contained in the English Companies Act of 1867 and from that act it was copied into most of the provincial acts. I have just had an opportunity of looking at Palmer's Company Precedents, thirteenth edition, 1927, page 574, and I find that that section was repealed in England and now under section 88 of the act of 1908

A contract and a return have to be filed within one month after the allotment of shares in whole or in part for a consideration other than cash.
That is about the same principle as was contained in the former act. But note this:
In case of default there is no provision that the shares are to be deemed to be allotted on a cash basis. Penalties are, however, imposed in case of default on officers of the company.
That is in case of default in the matter of filing the contract. Now in regard to this proposed amendment, subparagraph (a), to which the Minister of Railways has referred, provides in general terms for the same idea which is contained in provincial legislation, namely, the filing of a contract in order to show what the consideration was for the issue of shares. Subparagraph (b) I cannot find in the English act and I have never seen it before.
Paragraph Ob) or (c) ?

Paragraph (b). Paragraph (b), with all due respect to the Minister of Railways, is the one which, it seems to me, perpetuates the possibility of litigation and makes a pretty serious situation for anybody who buys shares no matter how innocently. It is one thing to insert in an act a provision that the directors shall not issue shares for a consideration other than cash unless they file with the registrar of joint stock companies a contract showing what those shares are issued for, whether for property or service. Then a man can go and buy the shares, and if he finds there is no contract he has a right to assume that the

St. Clair Transit Company
shares are issued for cash and that therefore the cash proceeds will be found in the treasury of the company. But it is quite another thing to say that not only shall there be a contract filed when the shares are issued for other than cash, but that the consideration for those shares shall be received and credited by the company at not more than its actual cash value. By the proposed subparagraph
(c)	if, in a company in which that provision has not been complied with, I buy shares ten years after the company is incorporated, I shall be liable to the company to make up in cash the par value of the shares notwithstanding the fact that I have paid in full for them already to the person from whom I bought them. The effect of it is this. I buy shares in the company from some other individual. The company was incorporated ten years ago. If the liquidator of the company can prove that ten years ago the directors of that company received certain property in consideration of the issue of shares, and that the value of that property was not the full par value of those shares, then I am liable to pay the difference.
The statute of limitations would apply if it was ten years ago.
Then let us say six years, although I do not think the statute of limitations would operate, because the action would accrue against me only from the time I purchased the shares.
The statute would run.

The statute would run
against me from the time the cause of action arises, but I do not think the cause of action arises against me until I become the owner of the shares. So I say that the effect of this would be that six years at least after the company had 'been incorporated and had issued its shares, for property or services which it turns out were not worth the full par value of the shares, and if the company fails, the liquidator of that company could come into the courts and cause me to pay up to the par value of those shares notwithstanding the fact that I had paid par for them to the person from whom I purchased them. That is going a long way in this sort of legislation; it is going further than any provincial act goes, and it seems to me that this house should stop and consider before arbitrarily passing such legislation, and particularly before putting it in the provisions of any particular bill when it is not the general law.
I know nothing about the merits of this particular legislation which is before the house, (but I do believe that we should not pass that sort of legislation without a good deal more consideration than we can give to it on the third reading of this bill.
Mr, IRVINE: Suppose the minister was going to buy shares as he has suggested, would he not be careful first to inquire how those shares had been acquired in the first place?

Certainly I would inquire. If the first part of the section were in force, I would go to the registrar of joint stock companies and there find out that the shares were issued, for instance, for services, perhaps six years before, but does my hon. friend tell me that I could be in a position to make up my mind what the court would decide five years afterwards as to the worth of those services? I would have to go back to the time those shares were issued and decide in my own mind whether the property or services for which they were issued was worth the amount of the shares? That burden should not be put upon any purchaser of shares.
It is on some of them now.
I do not know of any.
Where shares were issued under contracts filed with registrars of companies in the provinces where the old English act was in force, that risk was always present.
My hon. friend is quite wrong about that.
I have had to do it in my province.

The very case my hon. friend cited decided that so long as the contract was filed with the registrar of joint stock companies, and the directors of the company considered in good faith that the property was worth the amount of the shares issued, that decision was conclusive and would not be inquired into. My hon. friend, I think, is under a misapprehension about this. The individual is not required to try for himself any such question in that case. I say that my hon. friend's amendment, Mr. Speaker, goes far beyond anything I know in the English statutes and far beyond anything in the provincial statutes. Further than that, there is no provision even with regard to filing a contract under our Federal Companies Act.

There ought to be.
St. Clair Transit Company
I may agree with my hon. friend. The leader of the opposition is quite right that a prospectus is required to be filed, but there is no provision for the filing of the contract.

One of the questions
asked in the prospectus is, what contracts are there.

I understand that, but
that is very different from saying that the shares shall be taken as issued for a cash consideration. My hon. friend from Wetaski-win raises the real point. It seems to me it would be worth while considering in this house at some time an amendment to the general company law of this Dominion, putting into that law a provision similar to the one they have in the provinces, and I for one will be very ready to consider such a proposition when it is made, but I do not think we should select any particular bill as the one into which to put this special provision, when, after all, it is a matter of general company legislation.

Mr. Speaker, I am not opposed to this bridge in the same way that I am opposed to a bridge on the Niagara frontier. There may be a reason for this bridge; there is none for the other. There is no other bridge where the promoters desire to erect this bridge.

May I call the attention of hon. members who are yet to speak that there is an amendment before the house, and that they should address themselves to

Militia Pension Act
the merits of the amendment, not to the general principle of the bill? I had intended to bring this to the notice of the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat (Mr. Ryck-man).
Mr. Speaker, you have been pretty lenient with some hon. members who have spoken. I will try to keep within the four corners of the amendment.
I have no doubt that the hon. gentleman will do so.

In my judgment this is a proper amendment. In addition to the reasons already advanced in its favour, I wish to place before the house other reasons for its adoption. In this bill it is provided that eventually the bridge is to revert to the Dominion or to the province of Ontario. When that happens I do not want it to be encumbered with a lot of watered stock. Of course, members of the government will assure me, as some have already, that they are not behind the bill, but it will be noticed that with one or two exceptions they have all been helping its passage. I contend that the amendment is fair and proper and, to a certain extent at least, will prevent the watering of stock. Will the minister tell me what harm can come to this or to any other company by inserting in the charter a provision that the company must get cash only for its stock?

I have endeavoured to point out that the harm can come to people who purchase shares and are not in a position accurately to judge what a court will decide as to the value of the consideration for which the shares were issued.
Why a court?
Because that is the only way in which the penalty under (c) can be enforced.

The officers of the company can obviate all trouble in reference to the stock if they issue it for cash only. We want to prevent the giving away of shares in exchange for something that is of no value; that is, the watering of the stock. As I have already pointed out, my particular interest in this bill is that it purports to give something back to the country a little later on.
Did my hon. friend ever yet vote in this house for a bill which provided that shares could be issued only for cash?

I have no doubt that I
have done so, but I am prepared to say now that I am no longer in favour of this sort of thing, and in the future I shall vote against it, even if I stand alone in my opposition.

Mr. Speaker, I gather from the remarks of the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) and other members on the government side that they are quite in sympathy with the idea embodied in the amendment, but do not believe that it is practicable. The main objection of the minister seems to be that some ten years hence the question may be raised and the stockholders at that time may be held liable to the company or its creditors for the value of their holdings not paid in cash. It strikes me that if the minister is so much interested-

Mr. Smoke moves,
seconded by Mr. Dickie, that the debate be now adjourned.
He has not moved that.

Does the hon. member
object to the motion for adjournment of the debate?

He did not move any
motion.
Then the bill will fall to the bottom of the order paper.
It is nine o'clock.
The hour for private bills is exhausted.	.
The house resumed consideration in committee of Bill No. 197, to amend the Militia Pension Act-Mr. Ralston-Mr. Johnston in the chair.

When the committee rose we were considering section 5, and I intimated then that I would move an amendment. I explained the subsection intended to benefit those dependants, other than wives and children, of men who had served their full pensionable period but on account of whose death nothing was payable because they had left neither wife nor child. A suggestion was made that the use of the word "dependant" might be somewhat ambiguous, and I have therefore redrafted the section which I submitted this afternoon.
The word "dependant" does not appear in section 5.

Not as printed, but I read before recess a proposed amendment. The first subsection of that amendment as I gave it then remains; the second subsection I have
Militia Pension Act

redrafted, adding a few words descriptive of "dependant". The redrafted subsection 4 reads:
If an officer dies leaving no widow or child to whom a gratuity under the provisions of the preceding subsection, or a pension or compassionate allowance under this act would be payable, but who leaves a father, mother, brother, sister or child who, at the date of such officer's death was wholly or partially dependent on him for support the governor in council may grant to the person or persons so dependent a gratuity not exceeding in the aggregate the amount of the deductions made under subsection one of section ten of this act from the officer's pay during his services.
Is there not a possible incongruity there? The word "child" is used in the preceding subsection, meaning one under eighteen years of age.

True, the word "child" is used in both subsections. If the child is under eighteen then he or she comes under other sections providing for pensions to children. But there may be a child over eighteen dependent upon the father for support, and in that case he or she comes under the second subsection.
This would apply even to a married daughter.
Yes, if dependent upon the father for support.

I see no reason why the amendment should not pass, inasmuch as it merely permits the governor in council to hand over to certain named persons money which belonged to the officer, which was deducted from his salary or compensation in his lifetime, which he could not get, and which is now made available for those persons. I would point out however that the retroactive feature is an invitation to a request for similar legislation in other cases. It is exceptional and involves a principle which I am sure will be invoked hereafter by others in connection with the mounted police, and under other statutes. Once you concede the right to make this provision effective as from June, 1923, you will certainly be asked to extend the same consideration to others.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: You probably will.

Yes, you probably will. I cannot see on general principles that there is anything wrong with the section except that it has not been customary in this parliament to adopt this retroactive feature. This covers a special case, and one which no doubt is deserving; we are providing that the provision shall be retroactive over a period of five years. But I warn the minister-and I use the word
rMr. Ralston.]
"warn" this time in its proper sense-that many similar applications will come before
parliament. I remember having heard the same question discussed once before in the House of Commons, and the minister of the day thought it was too dangerous a thing to do when dealing with gratuities and pensions; for once you make legislation retroactive in respect of gratuities and pensions-fixing the year 1923, as in this case-there will be someone here next session saying, "I am willing to have you make it 1926". Others will say that 1924 will do. The minister should be able to devise some other method, and I should be glad to co-operate with him to meet the cases he has in mind. That, I think, would be preferable to putting on the statute books an invitation to all and sundry, affected either directly or indirectly, to ask for legislation of a retroactive character. I have in mind particularly a case I mentioned to the Minister of Justice last year in connection with the mounted police. In respect of the widow of an officer an effort was made to pass a measure retroactive for a year, and there was a good deal of discussion about it. I bring this matter to the attention of the minister because T think it is my duty to do so.

I thoroughly agree with
my hon. friend as to the undesirability of passing retroactive legislation, but in this instance it is, I think, amply justified, not by the circumstances of the individual case, but by this fact: Up to the thirtieth of June. 1923, the wife of a soldier could get a pension if that soldier had served for ten years; but on the thirtieth of June of that year that privilege ceased, so that while the woman whose husband had served ten years and died the day before could receive a pension, the widow of the man with similar service who died on the first of July found herself deprived of her allowance. In the event of an officer dying before he attains the pensionable period this provision will enable the widow to receive the amount deducted from his salary. I think therefore that the retroactive feature is justified, not, as I say, because of individual reasons but because it will, if I may use the expression, ease off the sharp break that took place when the new legislation was passed 'n June, 1923.
Section 5 agreed to.
On section 6-Term of service of militiaman.

During the course
of the discussion of this bill I inquired of the minister whether he had received any communications. I have one from a member of

Militia Pension Act
the permanent force asking that consideration be extended to some of them who have served continuously, but in another department of the government. I thought that service should go towards their pension in the same way as the service of these reservists would be estimated.	I (have 'too
objection to the first part, but here is a suggestion from one of our own men who since the war has joined the permanent force and has served continuously in some department of the government. He thinks the same favour should be granted to them as is granted to the other people referred to in the present bill.

The point is this: A civil servant joins the permanent force, and my friend suggests that the time during which he was a member of the civil service but not in the militia department should count as part of his service. I think that is not an unreasonable request, having regard to the fact that we are extending this to service in the constabulary, the navy and the air force, as well as to other services. After all, if a man was a civil servant paying into the superannuation fund, it seems to me that that time should count in the new branch of the civil service in which he finds himself.
I think that is dealt with in section 2, although I am bound to say that I speak with some hesitation as to that.

I cannot make it
out from this, but they evidently do not consider that it covers their case.
This afternoon I thought that was the very thing we were endeavouring to do in section 2, is that clear?

I thought so also, but
I am bound to say that I did not differentiate between the outside and the inside service. I shall be glad to look into this question.

Under the Civil Service
Superannuation Act the time served will apply towards a pension, but if that civil servant enlisted, even though he became a commissioned officer, he would not come under this section because this is an officers' section.

I will look into that
question.

Section agreed to.
On section 7-Pension to officer or militiaman of His Majesty's Army Reserve who enlisted in permanent force.

I endeavoured to explain
section 7 quite fully the other day; it deals with those cases of reservists who served with
the British army and were afterwards placed on the British army reserve. They then enlisted in the Canadian permanent force and were liable to be sent back to England at the outbreak of the war. Their services were requested by the British authorities, but the Canadian authorities asked that they remain here, and that request was granted. These men are now asking that some provision be made for accepting the time they served under the British colours, with the British army and with the reserve, for pension. Provision is made to add their service in Great Britain to their service in Canada up to the time they were demobilized, and they are given the same pension they would have received ii they had served in England, with the alternative of taking the Canadian pension from the time they started to serve in Canada.

I endorse the principle of
this section, but I cannot understand the words:
An officer or militiaman who, whilst belonging to His Majesty's Army Reserve, enlisted in the permanent force ....
Why should it be "officer or militiaman;" surely it would not be necessary for one of the reservists to be an officer or militiaman when he enlisted in the permanent force?

No, I do not think that is what is meant. An officer or militiaman is defined in the act, as my hon. friend will notice, as follows:
An officer or militiaman means a noncommissioned officer or private of the force.
This section says he is entitled to this option.

My point is that he might
be a reservist but not an officer or militiaman.
I do not think it is intended that he shall be contemporaneously an officer or militiaman and one of His Majesty's army reservists. He becomes an officer or militiaman when he enlists.

Section agreed to.
On section 8-Provision of 1919, c. 61, to apply to certain cases.

This section also I explained previously, quite fully. It provides for those members of the permanent force who served in the war and who were invalided out on account of war disabilities or sickness before July, 1919, when the act came into force which permitted them to retire even though they had only served ten years. It is said that the effect of their war disability was that they were out of the force before that section
Militia Pension Act

came into effect and this provision is to make them come under the provisions of that legislation as though they were members of the force at that time, in order that they may get their pension.

Section agreed to.
On section 9-Application to Royal Canadian Navy.

The other day there was some discussion with regard to deserted wives, and I think this a convenient time to discuss that matter; I promised to consider the question, and I think I have a suggestion which will meet with the approval of the committee. Under the superannuation act the deserted wife of an ex-civil servant gets no gratuity or payment; that payment is made to the husband, but I find that in the Pension Act relating to war disabilities there was an administration section inserted when the act was passed in 1919, which gave the Board of Pension Commissioners quite wide powers in appointing someone to administer a pension. Perhaps hon. gentlemen do not know that the pensions dealt with by this act are also paid by the Board of Pension Commissioners, although they do not decide the right of pay, ment, which is a matter for the governor in council. The Board of Pension Commissioners act as paying agents for the department.
For all military pensions.
Yes; and I am proposing that we insert in this act an administration section, similar to the section to which I have referred.
There was a good deal of trouble in working out that section, as I had occasion to discover at one time.

I have discussed the matter with the chairman of the Board of Pension Commissioners and he assures me that this . section has worked very satisfactorily in connection with disability pensions. In my discussion with the chairman of the Board of Pension Commissioners he assured me that, although they did not ask for any further responsibility than they now have, yet they have found that section to work out very well in that connection with disability pensions, and they would be prepared to take on if desired similar duties in connection with service pensions. I have endeavoured therefore in the section which I propose to make the Board of Pension Commissioners the recommending authority, and to provide that when the Board of Pension Commissioners

recommend, the minister may order the appointment of a person to administer the pension. I have used the same words as in section 16 of the Pension Act except that I have substituted the minister for the board in the operative portion of the section. If the committee will allow me, I will read it now. The provision is:
9. The following section is inserted after section 34:
_ 34a. When the Board of Pension Commissioners o,f_ Canada is of opinion that the pensioner is incapable of expending or is not expending the pension in a proper manner, or that he is not maintaining the members of his family to whom he owes the duty of maintenance, the minister may order that the pension be paid to such person as it may appoint, in order that the money may be expended by such person for the benefit of the pensioner and the members of his family. The expenses connected with such payment, if any, shall be paid by the commission.
This is where my friend the minister of pensions and health will come in and perhaps have to provide the board with a little extra for the purpose of such expenses. I am saying that is the exact section 16 contained in the Disability Pension Act, except that the word "minister" is substituted for "board'".

In one case which came to my attention it was found that it does not pay the minister to pay the money directly to the widow-you observe the way in which it is put. Might it not be better if the board recognized that the money be paid directly to the person thus entitled instead of to the administrators?

I agree with my hon. friend, and if I had been drafting a new section I would have done it that way. It
is really one of their own people who acts as agent in the district where the man happens to be living; he administers the fund and he pays it for the wife and children. It is because we have a practice which is already settled that it seems to me it would be better possibly to adopt this than to attempt to lay down something new.
Do I understand that the minister says that the pension is not paid directly to the widow and children in the case of disability pensions?

No. What the Board of Pension Commissioners do is go through the form of appointing someone to administer the pension, but the one they appoint is generally their own respresentative in that district.

This will be a very great step forward. In the case to which the member for Kingston (Mr. Ross) referred the

Forest Reserves and Parks Act
other day, and which I fancy most of the members of this house have had brought to their attention, the pensioner is out of the country and t'he wife is left in destitute circumstances. This will enable the payment to be made under the Pension Act. It is a great improvement on the old condition, and I think it is worthy of being tried out.
The minister will find that the cases to which I have referred, while not numerous, are very deserving cases. The amendment, I think, will work out satisfactorily.

I think it will in practice, because I have talked it over quite fully with the Chairman of the Board of Pension Commissioners. I am going to move. Mr. Chairman, that that be inserted as section 34A of the act. My hon. friend will see that part II follows; it should be in the first part and then will be made applicable automatically to parts II and III.
Why do you not make it a new section 9?

I will have to make it
section 9 of the act. I will have to renumber them.
Then say " the following section is inserted as "-
As section 34A.
Amendment agreed to.

speechtext: Shall part II of section 9 carry?

Section agreed to.
On section 10.

That should be renumbered. The section which you just read previously, introducing part II, should be renumbered as section 10, the section which you have just passed. The next one, on page 5, will be section 11.

speechtext:
Hon. CHARLES STEWART (Minister of the Interior) moved the second reading of Bill No. 193, to amend the Dominion Forest Reserves and Parks Act.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Johnston in the chair.
On section 1-Withdrawals from forest reserves.

maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Will the minister give an explanation?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I might
make an explanation of the whole bill. The bill proposes no additions to the forest reserves. These are withdrawals that have been recommended, after inspection by our officers who do land inspection work, as being lands that were included in the forest reserves and are fit for agricultural settlement. There is one withdrawal in Manitoba, the remainder being in Saskatchewan, and none in Alberta or British Columbia. Application, I may say, has been made to homestead these lands, and we are withdrawing them for the purpose of allowing them to be used for agricultural purposes.

maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Is it the policy of the department to withdraw from forest reserves lands that are fit for agriculture and apply them as homesteads?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Yes, with the single exception that sometimes we have applications for lands within the centre of a forest reserve, but my hon. friend will readily understand that it would not be feasible to allow settlement in the centre of a forest reserve, even where there is good agricultural land. Wherever good agricultural land is found on the boundary of a forest reserve, it is the policy of the department to withdraw it from the reserve. These lands are all on the boundaries.

maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: When these lands are withdrawn, what steps are taken in regard to allowing homesteading privileges? Will everyone have the same chance?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Yes, they are advertised as being open for homesteading.

maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: In that case the returned men will have the preference the same as they do now?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
This raises a very serious question, as perhaps the minister knows. After much consideration these lands are put into a forest reserve, and in some instances that has been done by order in council. It has been provided by the statutes of Canada that lands thus placed within a forest reserve by order in council cannot be taken out of that reserve

Forest Reserves and Parks Act
except by statute. That is the present law. The minister says that they have reports covering all these lands, which, except for one group which is in Manitoba, are all in Saskatchewan. Next week the minister is undertaking a great effort in connection with preventing the destruction of forests by fire. The public have been accustomed to these lands being part of a forest reserve, and it is true that a considerable area on the edge of the forest is free from trees and that this constitutes or has constituted a great bulwark against the attack on the forest itself by fire. The planting of homesteads near the forests-and while I was not able to trace them carefully on the maps, some of these come quite close to the forest itself-increases in a marked degree the fire hazard with respect to these areas. If we are sincere in our efforts to protect the forests, if they are of the value that the minister has intimated in connection with next week's campaign, and if we are reciprocating with the people of the United States in our efforts, this statute will at least increase the fire hazard of the forest reserves in Saskatchewan by not less than fifty per cent-and I think that is a conservative estimate-because, as the matter stands now, the fringe of forest in the reserve is protected by a strip of agricultural land. My understanding from the little checking up I was able to do is that these lands do not comprise sections within the reserve; that they all lie on the outskirts, and that they constitute one of the greatest safeguards we have against fire.

maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Are they prairie lands?

maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: They are mixed lands. The hon. member knows that is too large a question to expect me to give an answer that will be of value to him. Some of them are practically prairie lands and some are scrub lands, but there is no habitation upon them.

maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
My experience
in western Canada is that as habitation increases, the risk of fire decreases.
* Mr. BENNETT: That is true as regards prairie fires, but need I say to the hon. member' for Weyburn that these strips of arable land surrounding a forest reserve are very carefully safeguarded by the fire guardians. They bum them, for instance, at certain seasons of the year so as to protect from fire the forest that lies beyond. I fancy that my hon. friend has seen just what I mean with respect to that. These forest reserves are being.protected by aeroplanes, telephones and fire guards. I noticed particularly that that
[Mr. Bennett. 1
was the case in British Columbia and in some parts of my own province of Alberta They string lines along the trees for the purpose of carrying on telephonic communication, and they have depots from which they are able to make observations with respect to the cause of fires and immediately to take steps to protect the forests from destruction. There is no doubt that this fringe of untreed, arable land, when properly burned for purposes of protection and without habitation, constitutes a great safeguard with respect to the forests. From that standpoint I felt that we should have complete information because the area we are now withdrawing amounts to thirty-two square miles.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: That is out of all the reserves.

maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Yes. The area involved amounts to thirty-two square miles which, roughly speaking, is about twenty thousand acres. From a settlement standpoint that is not a large area scattered over Saskatchewan and Manitoba in all these reserves. It comprises only a limited number of homesteads. There are only four to the square mile, so that in an area of thirty-two square miles there would be about one hundred and twenty-eight homesteads in all. I am questioning the minister as to whether the benefit that accrues from a mere designation of these lands as agricultural lands for one hundred and twenty-eight homesteads is to be compared with the resultant risk that attaches of the destruction of the forests which we are doing so much to save, especially in the western provinces. I merely put the matter before the minister. I have not any expert evidence to support my point beyond a mere inspection of the map and a determination of the areas, but what we have to face is this: Is it desirable to render subject to fire hazards to a very much greater degree than now exists the forests affected in Saskatchewan, Alberta and Manitoba, for the sake of rendering open for settlement one hundred and twenty-eight quarter sections of land? That is the proposition. I think the minister should give us some information with respect to that question so far as he is able to give it.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I shall be
very glad to do that, Mr. Chairman. I think my hon. friend is unduly alarmed about the fire hazard, because these eliminations are alongside of the forest reserves. They do not involve a very large area except in one instance, where the most we are taking is twenty-one square miles. We do not increase *h* ire hazard by taking these lands that

Forest Reserves and Parks Act
are fit for agricultural purposes owing to the fact that the forest reserves in many instances, particularly in Manitoba, are settled right up to the boundary of the reserve. That is the case in many of the forest reserves in Saskatchewan. It is not the case in the more northern districts, but we have not yet selected forest reserves in what are strictly the unsettled parts of the country. They will have to be selected later on, and the endeavour will be to select for the forest reserves lands that are unfit for agricultural purposes, and every precaution will be taken to protect them from destruction by fire. I want to relieve my hon. friend's mind of any anxiety that by the elimination of small areas on the fringes of the forest reserves we are increasing the fire hazard.

maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: You are bound to increase the fire hazard.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: No, because these lands are settled right up to the boundary of the reserve, and the taking of a small additional portion of the land for agricultural purposes does not in any degree increase the fire hazard.

maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
It puts the fire that
much nearer the forest.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: But settlement is right up to the boundary of the reserve.

maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: And now you are changing the boundary.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
We are
not changing the boundary. The settlement to-day is up to the reserve in the great-majority of cases, and in some cases unfortunately they get into the reserve.

maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I know that, and fire
happens by reason of it.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: These small areas that are desirable for agricultural purposes are, I think, much better in the hands of some careful farmer than allowed to lie uncultivated with grass growing to a considerable height, with the risk some day of a prairie fire coming along. That is the menace. Personally, speaking from my own experience, I would much prefer to have the boundary of the reserve in the thickly timbered areas, because then we have a much better chance of preventing the fire from entering from outside.

maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: None of these lands will be offered for sale?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: No, they will all be opened for homesteading.

maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: I trust that the particulars given here have all been carefully checked.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Yes.

Section agreed to.
Sections 2 to 8 inclusive agreed to.
Bill reported, read the third time and passed.

maintopic: REPORTED LANDING OF GERMAN PLANE "BREMEN" ON GREENLY ISLAND

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: REPORTED LANDING OF GERMAN PLANE "BREMEN" ON GREENLY ISLAND
speechtext:
Before we proceed to the
next order, Mr. Speaker, the Minister of National Defence has received an important intimation which I think will be of special interest to all -hon. members of this house, and I would ask that he might now have permission to announce it.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. L. RALSTON (Minister of National Defence):
maintopic: REPORTED LANDING OF GERMAN PLANE "BREMEN" ON GREENLY ISLAND
speechtext:
We have had so many rumours,
Mr. Speaker, that one almost hesitates to say anything with regard to the intrepid fliers who yesterday morning, started out from Ireland on a transatlantic flight to this continent, but this report which I have received seems to be reasonably official. It reads:
Plane forced down in snowstorm on Greenly island. Reported by Point Amour wireless station. Official. Lighthouse on island and keeper there to take care of fliers.
Upon looking at the map I find that Greenly is in the straits of Belle Isle, and it is rather significant to note that it is just over the Canadian line and in the province of Quebec.

maintopic: REPORTED LANDING OF GERMAN PLANE "BREMEN" ON GREENLY ISLAND
speechtext: And not far from Gaspe, either.

Is the agreement signed

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:

I know that in most
